speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The "School Strike for Climate" movement led by 16-year-old, Greta Thunberg, has inspired millions of students worldwide to push their governments to take action.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But at the same time, Hong Kong is burning.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Youth-led mass protests, while at first peaceful, have since degenerated into lawlessness and violence.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The potential and energy of the youths are clear.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The only question is to what end that potential will be turned into.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: In September, Yale-NUS College (YNC) cancelled a Learning Across Boundaries programme titled "Dialogue and Dissent in Singapore".

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The programme was organised by Singapore playwright Mr Alfian Sa'at.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The reasons for cancellation have been addressed during Question Time today.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: What I am concerned with are the conclusions that some have drawn from the episode.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Mr Goh Choon Kang, a former Member of Parliament, wrote in Lianhe Zaobao on 18 September to critique the YNC programme.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: His article was titled “Singapore does not need a "colour revolution." His concern is that the programme would expose students to Singaporean political dissidents, whom he argues are a subversive or improper political influence.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: He is concerned that impressionable students may be incited to destabilise Singapore.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: I do not want to single Mr Goh out.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: His concerns are shared by many Singaporeans who are concerned about the principles and objectives of a liberal education, and the risk of such an education being subverted for non-academic ends.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: At the risk of simplifying, what is really being questioned is whether our students are being enlightened by their education or corrupted by it.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: From time to time, nations must hang a philosopher to encourage the others.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Socrates, the founder of Western philosophy, was put to death for corrupting the youths of Athens.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: What is profoundly uncomfortable to many of us is the possibility that students will be taught something that is untrue; if not untrue, then, even worse, an inconvenient truth; and that once equipped with these ideas, they will be incited to put their ideals in action.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But in fact, a liberal education aims to do nothing of the kind.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Like other philosophies of education, a liberal education simply aims to cultivate a good human being and citizen.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: What is distinctive is that a liberal education holds the student responsible for their own intellectual development.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: A good liberal education teaches the student that the truth is something to be discovered rather than something imparted by a wise sage; that no writing, statement or deed, should pass without critical questioning; that, as Socrates said, "the unexamined life is not worth living".

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: If, as a result of education, the student discovers that some social injustice exists and develops a conviction that they have a responsibility to set it right, then that is a consequence, but not the aim, of a liberal education.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Our hon Member, Mr Mohamed Irshad, founded Roses of Peace as a student, as an inter-faith youth movement to counter religious hatred with love and kindness.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Mr Lim Jingzhou, a Yale-NUS student, co-founded the Cassia Resettlement Team, a youth-led collective which supports resettled elderly and vulnerable residents through house visits and building community networks.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: We should critically question the false dichotomy separating the activist from the volunteer, where we often treat the former with suspicion while showering the latter with praise.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Both are the result of putting values into action.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The concern remains that who teaches and what is taught in the classroom can shape our youths for good or for ill.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: This morning, the Minister for Education explained that we must account for personal character, behaviour and ideology when assessing potential educators.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Reasonable people will agree there are some ideologies so hostile or behaviours so reprehensible that we must protect the youths by preventing exposure.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But in making such judgements, we must guard against unnecessarily narrowing minds in the guise of protecting them.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The story of Socrates reminds us that what is politically convenient – to university administrators, to the public, or to the Government – is not always what is truthful or right.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: In the case of Mr Alfian, although we may agree he is not the ideal academic instructor of political dissent, I would hope that we judge his award-winning poems and plays still worthy of study as Singapore literature; that his skills as a playwright and artistic mentor can still benefit our youths.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: As Max Weber noted, the academic has a duty to discover the truth and to force society to confront those truths.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But the pursuit of truth is different from acting on it, especially in the classroom.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: This is not because activism is wrong, but because the student should be tested on their ability to discern the truth and not on whether their values align with those of the instructor.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: My academic colleagues who have been called activists, such as Assoc Prof Teo You Yenn, understand this principle well.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: They have distinguished themselves both with their scholarship and with their activism.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: If we are put to the test by public opinion, we must have the courage to choose to open minds rather than to close them.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Rather than back down, we must pursue their inquiry with the highest standards of scholarship and teaching.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: If we ask for unrealistic perfection in our critical academics, our scholars will be biased towards the safe and the status quo.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: This is a hidden danger that threatens us all.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: It encourages a sloppiness of thinking, a belief that it is safer to regurgitate received wisdom than to seek new answers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: This will be bad for our youths and bad for Singapore.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Courses in the liberal education tradition are faculty-intensive and highly demanding.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But a narrow focus on costs blinds us to the possibilities of a liberal education.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Our democracy is at risk if the electorate is unable to critically assess facts, policies and ideas, leading to the politics of fear and misinformation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: This is a citizenship skills gap that a liberal education addresses.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: A well-designed liberal education will allow weaker students to develop their critical reading, writing and speaking skills in a safe space.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: For example, the National University of Singapore (NUS) University Scholars Programme and YNC, aim to push the intellectual boundaries of their students, and so they are highly selective to ensure rigour and quality.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But if we believe that a liberal education has benefits for active citizenship, then we should make offerings available to more students.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Beyond education, I believe that Singaporeans in general will gain much if they adopt the liberal values of open mindedness tempered by critical inquiry to deal with the complexities of a changing world.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: I do not mean that people should adopt so-called "Western" liberal social or political attitudes, although I draw no adverse inferences there.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Rather, we must accept, as a society and as individuals, that there is a right to question ideas, beliefs and policies, and to have one's own ideas and actions be questioned, critically but respectfully.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: If we can recognise the importance of these values for Singapore in an uncertain future, we will see that a liberal education, far from corrupting the youths, provides a source of strength for the future.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Ms Anthea Ong, do you wish to say something?

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Yes, Ms Anthea Ong, are you speaking on the Adjournment Motion?

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: Do I speak from here or can I go to the rostrum?

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: They are passionate and committed to a more democratic, more politically engaged and more inclusive way of moving Singapore forward.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: Deputy Prime Minister Heng Swee Keat’s words at Singapore Summit 2019 acknowledged the need to include our youths.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: He said, "For young people especially, being able to actively shape the future of our nation and playing a part to build this future is key to growing their sense of ownership and commitment to Singapore." However, does our political landscape give them the space to realise this vision?

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: At the recent SG Climate Rally organised by university students, Singaporeans spoke up to urge the Government to adopt more structural solutions to the climate crisis.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: One of the rally organisers, however, admitted the difficulty in speaking up.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: She said that when asked to speak at Speakers' Corner, she feared being put on a "blacklist".

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: Another young advocate doing work in the social sector also shared about fears that the Government would choose to penalise their organisation if they spoke about issues they see on the ground.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: Many young Singaporeans I spoke to collectively shared concerns on the limited public space for citizens to participate in discussion, debate and dissent without the constant presence of fear, surveillance and coercion, real and imagined.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: These feelings of paranoia and suspicion must not be simply dismissed.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: When citizens become too afraid of the repercussions to speak up and when critics become too cynical to engage, Singapore would suffer a great loss.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: When that day comes, only a narrow range of ideas will dominate, group-think will prevail and we will lose the dream of a diverse, inclusive and democratic Singapore.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: We must not confuse those who insult with those who critique.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: Let us not underestimate the value of our youths speaking up and taking action to make change.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: Then, there is the Community for Advocacy and Political Education (CAPE), a student group based at Yale-NUS that builds capacity and political literacy for effective and constructive active citizenry with a range of important civic projects and initiatives, including producing infographics on the Protection from Online Falsehoods and Manipulation Act (POFMA) and the "brownface" issue, as well as organising political education workshops with schools and Members of Parliament.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: Cassia Resettlement Team – my fellow Nominated Member of Parliament Assoc Prof Walter Theseira had mentioned – is a ground-up non-profit powered mostly by youths, blending community and advocacy work to support residents through a range of interconnected issues, such as poverty, public housing relocation, ageing, mental health and end-of-life issues.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: The Inter-University Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual Transgender (LGBT) Network, a collection of student groups in Singapore universities to collaborate in fostering safer and more inclusive school communities for everyone regardless of sexual orientation, gender identity and expression.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: There is Advocates for Refugees, a ground-up movement consisting of mainly youths advocating and raising consciousness for the cause of refugees.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: Singapore Youth Voices for Biodiversity facilitates youth discussions on topics, such as habitat preservation and development, and then channels these inputs to the Convention on Biological Diversity's international conferences and stakeholder processes.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: All these groups, almost completely youth-led, are invested in the principle of deliberative and shared democracy in order to co-create a shared and inclusive Singapore they want to be a part of.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: The Government should re-evaluate their attitudes towards advocacy, activism and dissent.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: They should learn to embrace these actions as long as they come from a place of good faith.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: The narrative must move beyond "activists as troublemakers".

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: One must not arbitrarily draw the line between "good" and "bad" activists based solely on the topics they speak up on.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: To that end, all Singaporeans, from advocates, critics, dissenters, artists, intellectuals, writers, community organisers to "ordinary" citizens have their own experiences to contribute and form an important and untapped resource in Singapore’s style of governance.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: Take, for instance, the Government's response to the Singapore Climate Rally.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: While the organisers had painstakingly put together a "Call to Action" in the hope for concrete policy follow-up, the Government's only response was to commend the organisers.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: Our young citizens are concerned about the asymmetry between youths who work tediously to engage the Government and the Government's perfunctory and lukewarm response.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: Youths should also be able to choose their representation on the Youth Action Panel.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: We should also work to educate the public on national issues, help break down complex information and ensure they are well explained to citizens so that as many people as possible may contribute.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: Political literacy should be a goal the fourth generation (4G) leadership strives towards. "The surest way to corrupt a youth is to instruct him to hold in higher esteem those who think alike than those who think differently," said German philosopher Friedrich Nietzsche.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: I am impressed by their brilliance and moved by their commitment and love for Singapore.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: To turn many of these critical young lovers away and deny them their say would be a great loss for our country.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: Let us give our young ones space to challenge, roots to lead and reasons to stay.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: I did not realise you were making such a long clarification.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: I should have let you speak from the rostrum.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Minister Ong Ye Kung has addressed many of the points the Member has raised.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: First, the importance of separating academia and activism in the classroom; and, second, the value of liberal arts education and critical inquiry.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: I will also talk about the importance of academic freedom existing within the context of our social norms.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Senior Minister of State Sim Ann will subsequently respond to Ms Anthea Ong and also to some of the issues raised by Assoc Prof Walter Theseira.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: This is not to say that academics should only be constrained to writing papers for publications.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Academics are strongly encouraged to translate their work into real world impact, be it through technological innovations or public policy recommendations.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: This is also not to say that all classes need to be about open-ended inquiry.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: There is significant space for applied learning and teaching of practical skills.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: But these should be guided by the objectives of education and learning and the acquisition of competencies that prepare students for work.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Second, our universities should provide a space where different ideas and perspectives are explored and objectively and rigorously debated.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Indeed, a key attribute of liberalism is a spirit of tolerance, openness and acceptance that different people may have different views.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Our educational institutions play a vital role in nurturing students into adults who are open-minded and can critically assess ideas, beliefs and policies put before them.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: And, likewise, be prepared for their own ideas and actions to be assessed, all in an objective and respectful manner.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: This is especially important in today’s age, where online falsehoods and manipulation can spread very quickly through social media information that they encounter.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: The essential skill that we want our students to learn is critical thinking, which is the foundation of any education programme of high academic standards and it is not limited to a liberal arts education.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: All of our educational institutions nurture students to conduct critical thinking with maturity of thought and a sense of responsibility towards society, that is, to think critically, rather than, as Minister Ong Ye Kung put it, be unthinkingly critical.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: As the Member acknowledged, our universities today already have core curriculum components that develop critical thinking in students.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: We will work with the AUs to see how this can be further enhanced.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: But the AUs have their constraints, such as limited curriculum time to work with.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: At the secondary school and pre-university levels, critical thinking skills are also taught in Humanities subjects like Social Studies, which all students take.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Students examine issues by considering multiple perspectives and draw reasoned conclusions substantiated by evidence and sound values, such as intellectual integrity, respect for a diversity of views and an appreciation of the implications of their conclusions on society.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Even in countries with a strong culture of freedom of expression, speakers have been uninvited or pressured to withdraw from speaking engagements at universities due to the need to cater to the views of the community.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: For instance, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, then-Chief Minister of the state of Gujarat, was disinvited to an economic forum hosted by an American university in 2013 because of an online protest against him.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Former Managing Director of the International Monetary Fund, Christine Lagarde, was pressured to withdraw from speaking at an American college after students took issue with her alleged role in the failed developmental policies implemented in poorer countries.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: I am not passing any judgement on whether these decisions were wrong or right.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: But they show that even in the most liberal societies, academic freedom needs to exist within the norms and culture of the community.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: It is, therefore, important that our educational institutions abide by the principles that Minister Ong Ye Kung laid earlier in his speech.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: We will leave it to the universities on how they implement these principles.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: As academics, we all want to contribute in nurturing our students into adults who are open-minded, can critically assess ideas, beliefs and policies put before them, in addition to being competent in the areas that they may specialise in.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Education (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: I urge them to understand the principles, as shared by Minister Ong Ye Kung, and exercise sensible judgement.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Senior Minister of State Sim Ann, you have only six minutes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Sim Ann)
text: I also cannot help noticing that the concluding paragraphs of Ms Anthea Ong's speech very nicely answered the concerns that she raised at the start.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Sim Ann)
text: I believe that Members of the House who have heard the concluding paragraphs of her speech can only conclude that our youths, through her words, are passionate, energetic and quite uninhibited in speaking up.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Sim Ann)
text: I agree that such youths who wish to help shape the future of Singapore should have avenues for doing so.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Sim Ann)
text: This is, indeed, something that the Government has publicly committed to supporting.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Sim Ann)
text: The Ministry of Culture, Community and Youth (MCCY) has been actively engaging youths to better understand their views, aspirations and needs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Sim Ann)
text: We are heartened to see that our youths show a strong sense of purpose and care deeply about the long-term future of our country.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Sim Ann)
text: At the same time, we want to help our youths go beyond talking about the topics and causes that captivate their attention.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Good ideas need to be translated into action before they can result in concrete and positive change.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Such action can be taken by the youths themselves, in partnership with others or in partnership with the Government.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Sim Ann)
text: In the process of conceptualising and designing effective action, youths can gain a hands-on understanding of the responsibility that comes with advocating for change.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Sim Ann)
text: They would need to work out ways to inform, persuade and mobilise others in support of their cause.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Their chances of success would grow if they are open-minded and prepared to have their ideas and beliefs challenged, and if they are able to recognise and address the needs and perspectives of other segments of society.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Sim Ann)
text: MCCY encourages this through the design of the Youth Conversations.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Sim Ann)
text: It is a platform for our youths to articulate their ideas and vision for Singapore's future, and to create positive change.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Sim Ann)
text: The SG Youth Action Plan is led by a diverse group of youth leaders who have taken an inclusive approach to reach out to youths from different walks of life and from different educational and professional backgrounds.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Sim Ann)
text: The SG Youth Action Plan seeks to support youths in coming up with robust and impactful policy ideas and projects by equipping them with the information and resources they need.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Sim Ann)
text: In addition, we are bringing youth leaders to engage directly with Ministries on policy issues, such as sustainability.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Sim Ann)
text: In the next phase of nation-building, the Government will shift from working for citizens, to working with all segments of citizens.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Sim Ann)
text: SG Youth Action Plan is very much a part of this approach, which we have termed SG Together.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Sim Ann)
text: It is our hope that the SG Youth Action Plan will not only foster many projects undertaken by youths for the betterment of society but also develop skills among youths for engaging with the wider society and instil confidence in them that their ideas can be translated into action and, ultimately, make a positive difference.
